title: SALSA-V: Shortcut-Augmented Long-form Synchronized Audio from Videos
claim: A multimodal generator conditions a shared transformer on frozen encoder features and mixes streams through joint attention and adaptive normalization.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; dashed lines zoom a block into detail
description: A block diagram in two parts. On the left is the overall pipeline. Video frames feed frozen Sync and Semantic encoders, shown as blue and green boxes with snowflake icons. Text joins them through a summation node. Audio goes through a red VAE encoder, a noise-sum node, MMDiT-X blocks, DiT blocks and a red VAE decoder. Dashed arrows carry the conditioning signals. Dashed diagonal lines run from the MMDiT-X block to a zoomed-in panel on the right. That panel shows the block internals as two parallel streams, Semantic and Audio. Each stream has adaLN, joint attention, Conv, ConvMLP and residual sum nodes. A Linear and Self-Attention branch sits at the side. Rounded boxes labelled Global cond. and Local cond. mark where the conditioning enters. The eye goes first to the left-hand flow and the red trapezoids.
caption: Architectural diagram of SALSA-V. We utilize a mixture of modified MMDiT-X blocks operating jointly over the combined sequence of audio and semantic features, as well as single-stream DiT blocks, which operate on the latent representation of a VAE (red). The overall global conditioning signal consists of the text embedding and pooled semantic features (green), which are extracted from a pretrained SigLIP 2 encoder, synchronization features (blue) obtained from a dedicated contrastive model, and the time-step embedding. The local conditioning tensor equals the global conditioning summed to the sequence-aligned synchronization features.
abstract: We propose SALSA-V, a multimodal video-to-audio generation model capable of synthesizing highly synchronized, high-fidelity long-form audio from silent video content. Our approach introduces a masked diffusion objective, enabling audio-conditioned generation and the seamless synthesis of unconstrained length audio sequences. Additionally, by integrating a shortcut loss into our training process, we achieve rapid generation of high-quality audio samples in as few as eight sampling steps, paving the way for near-real-time applications without requiring dedicated fine-tuning or retraining. We demonstrate that SALSA-V significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both audiovisual alignment and synchronization with video content in quantitative evaluation and a human listening study. Furthermore, our use of random masking during training enables our model to match spectral characteristics of reference audio samples, broadening its applicability to professional audio synthesis tasks such as Foley generation and sound design.
